site.name: Tucson Mine Ruins
overview: The Tucson Mine was a substantial Iron Hill operation in the Leadville district. Historic accounts describe deep shaft development and later mining of silver, lead, zinc, and zinc-carbonate ores, while surviving heavy foundations and ore-handling remains indicate the scale of the surface plant.
The Tucson should be interpreted as one mine within the broader Iron Silver Mining Company landscape, not as a label for every nearby Iron Hill working.

timeline.text: The Tucson became one of the developed Iron Hill workings as Leadville operators expanded underground through shafts and inclines.
The Tucson shaft reached roughly 1,100 feet, reflecting substantial underground development.
Historic mining literature reported very high-grade silver assays from lower levels of the mine.
Considerable mining continued, with lead- and zinc-sulfide ores forming an important part of production.
Several attempts were made to reopen or sustain the property, but none produced a lasting revival.
The upper part of the shaft was reopened to reach a remaining zinc-carbonate, or smithsonite, ore body.
Large ore-bin remnants, dumps, and heavy hoist foundations remain useful identification clues for the former mine complex.

moreHistory: Iron Hill was one of Leadville’s major mining zones. The Tucson developed within a dense group of Iron Silver Mining Company properties where separate shafts and claims tapped related but locally complex ore bodies.

Historical descriptions of the Tucson emphasize the depth of the shaft and the changing character of the ore. Silver-rich material was reported from deeper levels, while lead and zinc sulfides became important during the 1910s.

The 1940 reopening targeted smithsonite, a zinc carbonate left from earlier mining. That episode shows how operators repeatedly reconsidered old workings when metal prices, processing methods, or knowledge of remaining ore changed.

Surviving surface features are especially useful for identification. Large ore-storage remnants and substantial concrete hoist foundations indicate that Tucson was not a minor prospect; it required heavy equipment to move ore and workers through a deep shaft system.
For Remnant, nearby Iron Hill mines should remain separate records. Shared ownership or underground relationships do not mean every surviving ruin belongs to the Tucson Mine.
